Write your answer to `/app/answer.md`.

terminal, and no other file, is read. If that file is missing or empty when you
stop, the task scores zero however good your analysis was.

You are working against a time limit and will be cut off without warning when it
is reached. So:

1. **Write a complete answer to `/app/answer.md` early** -- as soon as you have a

That way the file always holds your best answer so far, and being cut off costs
you refinement rather than the whole attempt. Answer in prose, and state each
point explicitly rather than implying it.

# The view from the driver's seat of the blue vintage Amilcar

## Verdict: No

**No — the driver does not have an unobstructed view of the crouching photographer at the lower-left edge of the frame.** Looking out of his cockpit towards that corner of the square, his line of sight runs into the flag marshal and, above all, into the huge red Swiss flag the marshal is sweeping across the front of the car.

## Establishing who and where the driver is

The blue car is the vintage Amilcar carrying race number 17, Swiss plate GL·8527 and Red Bull / "Jungfrau Stafette" stickers. Like period Amilcar racers it is right-hand drive, so the driver is the **man** — the one with the sunglasses pushed up on his head, sitting low behind the nearer of the two little curved aero-screens. Because the car is pointing at us, his right-hand seat appears on the **left** of the two occupants in the photograph; the blonde woman in sunglasses beside him is the passenger. The driver therefore sits on the side of the car that faces the photographer, and the sightline in question leaves the cockpit forwards and to the driver's right, dropping down towards the kneeling man at the bottom-left of the picture.

## What lies between them

Tracing that line outwards from the driver's eye, these things occupy it:

1. **The car's own front-end fittings.** First come the small curved perspex aero-screens and their wooden/alloy frame directly in front of him, and then — sitting almost exactly on the bearing to the photographer — the **round, chrome-backed rear-view mirror mounted on the driver's side of the scuttle**. Beyond that is the tall, unguarded front wheel and its exposed radius rod.

2. **The large red Swiss flag — the principal obstruction.** A big red flag with the white Swiss cross, mounted on a long pale wooden pole, is being swung across the nose of the car. It is strongly **motion-blurred** because it is moving fast, and it is unmistakably in front of the car: it covers the top of the near front tyre, the chrome radiator shell and part of the left-hand headlamp. Anyone in the cockpit looking towards the lower-left of the scene is looking into that sheet of moving red cloth.

3. **The marshal who is waving it.** The flag is held by an **elderly official seen from behind** — white polo shirt with black side panels, a blue "WTCC" baseball cap, cream trousers and red trainers. He is striding across the road in front of the car with his right arm fully extended along the pole, and his body, arm and the pole itself fill the strip of pavement that separates the car from the photographer. He is so close to the photographer that his left hand and hip actually overlap the photographer's lens in the frame.

4. **The red-and-white plastic barrier tape** strung across the square to hold the crowd back also crosses the same bearing.

5. **Behind the line rather than strictly on it, but filling the same direction of view:** the thick trunk of the plane tree, the advertising pillar, and the spectators behind the tape — among them a small girl in a white dress and turquoise sun hat.

## The photographer for reference

He is kneeling on one knee at the extreme lower-left, in a grey T-shirt and an olive photographer's vest, wearing sunglasses, with his eye to a DSLR that has a flashgun mounted on top. He is shooting rightwards at the car, from roughly two metres off its right-hand flank.

## An honest caveat about depth

Measuring the scene carefully supports a consistent reconstruction: the camera sits about 1.5 m above the ground with the horizon roughly a quarter of the way down the frame, and the figures' ground-contact points and head sizes agree with each other. On that reconstruction the marshal's shoes sit markedly lower in the frame than either the photographer's shoe or the car's front tyres, which puts him some 13–16 % nearer the camera — on the order of two to three metres closer than either. The photographer, meanwhile, kneels at almost exactly the same distance from the camera as the car's front axle.

So part of the overlap we see is a projection effect: strictly, the marshal and the flag are angled somewhat **in front of** the car rather than sitting precisely on the straight line from the driver's eye to the photographer's eye, and a fraction of that apparent blocking is the camera's viewpoint collapsing the depth. But the marshal is walking straight through that space and the flag is being swung through a wide arc across it, which is exactly why it is so badly smeared by motion blur. At the instant captured, the driver's view down to the crouching photographer is broken, not clear — and what breaks it is the red Swiss flag and the man carrying it, with the car's own aero-screen and scuttle mirror clipping the very start of the sightline.
